stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats, Ep. 7: The Anti-Fascist Fight For Affordability
stories.text: Democrats made affordability the centerpiece of their midterm campaigns and won big. But what if the cost-of-living crisis isn't just an economic issue? What if it's a democracy issue? In Episode 7 of Don't F#*k It Up, Democrats (watch above or here ) , David Sirota speaks with Isabella Weber, an economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and author of the new book Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy . Weber explains how economic insecurity fuels authoritarianism, how the corporate-friendly economic policies Democrats have championed for decades may have helped pave the way for Trump, and why delivering on affordability will require taking on some of the world's most powerful corporations. They explore what Democrats should actually do to bring down the cost of living and restore people's faith in democracy. stories.title: Palestinians in Gaza Are Lining Their Tents with Sandbags to Stop Israeli Bullets
stories.text: Tareq Abu Adhra fortifies a side of his makeshift shelter with sandbags to protect from Israeli gunfire, in the Bir 19 encampment in Khan Younis. Story by Mohamed Ahmed and Sharif Abdel Kouddous KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip—Nofal Al-Akhras filled another empty flour sack with sand, tied off the top, and heaved it onto the other bags lining the outside of his tent in the Bir 19 area of the southern Gaza Strip. A displacement camp in a desolate sandy expanse west of Khan Younis, Bir 19 lies close to the yellow line where occupying Israeli troops are stationed. Al-Akhras stacked the sandbags three high, at about waist level, among drying laundry hung on a sagging clothesline, forming a makeshift barrier—a desperate attempt to protect himself and his family from Israeli gunfire. “Every day, around the clock, we are caught off guard by stray, deadly bullets fired indiscriminately,” he told Drop Site News. “We have lost many loved ones who were martyred by stray bullets striking displacement tents for no reason whatsoever. stories.title: Democrats Want To Investigate Nvidia. Their Megadonor Is On The Board.
stories.text: At the recent post-election confab in Denver, Democratic leaders promised a new era of anti-corruption and accountability in Washington. But will those promises be fulfilled if those being held accountable have ties to Democrats themselves? Or is the infrastructure of elite impunity so bipartisan that the party is already compromised? That is now a live question after President Donald Trump pressed Nvidia’s board to unanimously vote to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang despite allegations that an extramarital affair may have compromised U.S. national security. The reinstatement — while Trump holds Nvidia stock and Nvidia funds the White House ballroom — has prompted Democrats in both the House and Senate to promise a corruption investigation once the new Congress convenes in January. “The decision by the Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang is indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible,” said likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY). “Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by Nvidia.” “We need to investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement,” tweeted Sen. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: Pod, Save Thyself
stories.text: I’d always wondered what the inside of the proverbial big tent looked like, that amazingly broad political space where supposedly every kind of Democrat links arms, from democratic socialists to the corporate donors of New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. And at Crooked Con, I got to glimpse it — or at least a corporate simulation of it. “The Big Tent” stage was the conference’s main attraction, the place where crowds packed in to watch some of the biggest names in Democratic politics. Crooked Con made it theatrical: a darkened room accommodating hundreds or thousands; blue-and-white American-flag-style stars projected onto the ceiling, and huge digital screens that faded from swing-state purple to cobalt blue (it’s a metaphor). Inherent in the stage’s name was also an instruction, a not-at-all-subtle call for one of establishment Democrats’ most urgent decrees: party unity. It sounds like a pleasant enough idea, but it’s a proposition that’s more complicated — and dangerous — than it looks. When I arrived at Crooked on Nov. 7, the energy was high. stories.text: In 2016, Richard Ojeda voted for Bernie Sanders in the primaries and Donald Trump in the general election. Now he's a Democrat headed to Congress David Sirota hosted a live conversation with Ojeda, discussing populism, what Democrats should do next, and what it takes to win voters who've stopped listening.
